title: Vayeshev: why so sad today? (Genesis 40:6–7)
hookLine: in prison, Joseph notices two sad faces and asks why
tomorrow: at the end of two years

lines: THE ONE WHO ALWAYS SAYS FINE.
cards: When did someone last ask how you were, and wait for the real answer? The coworker who always says fine, the friend who laughs a little too fast, the kid who goes straight to their room: they're easy to walk past.
Everyone has problems enough of their own. Joseph has more than his share. Potiphar's wife accused him of something he refused to do, and he's been thrown into prison.
Now he's the one looking after the other prisoners, including two of Pharaoh's officials: the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. One morning, he walks in.

teach.b: The two officials have each had a dream in the same night.
In the morning, the Torah says, Joseph came in, looked at them, and saw that they were troubled. The Hebrew word, zo'afim, means upset, stormy, out of sorts.
And Joseph asks them: why do your faces look so sad today? Stop there. Joseph is a prisoner himself: sold by his brothers, falsely accused, far from home.
He has every reason to be wrapped up in his own misery. Instead he notices two faces. Some readers love the word today in his question.
It means he knew what their faces usually looked like. He'd been paying attention all along, so he could see when something changed. They tell him: we dreamed, and there's nobody to interpret it.

Joseph answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" Tell me, please. The cupbearer tells his dream: a vine, three branches, grapes pressed into Pharaoh's cup.
In three days, Joseph says, you'll be restored. The baker's dream goes the other way. And all of it happens as Joseph said.
This is the hinge of Joseph's whole life. Two years later, that cupbearer will remember a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams, and Joseph will stand before Pharaoh.
His rise from prison to palace doesn't start with a miracle, or a clever plan. It starts with a question. A prisoner looks at two other prisoners and asks, what's wrong?

how: Jewish tradition counts receiving others with a pleasant face and noticing their distress as part of kindness, and Joseph's question in prison is taught as an example of it.

and he settled, the portion ending in prison

games.q: you're in prison, falsely accused. two fellow prisoners look miserable this morning. you're Joseph. what do you do?
o: keep to yourself: you have enough troubles.
ask them why they look so sad today.
tell them things could be worse.
games.why: Joseph asked why their faces were sad. that question led, two years later, to Pharaoh's palace.

practice: Bring to mind the faces you saw yesterday, family at breakfast, a coworker, a cashier, a neighbor, and whether anyone looked more tired, quieter, stormier than usual.
Pick one, and picture asking gently: you seem a little off today, how are you really? Then picture just listening.
